idiom_name: kotlinx.serialization Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true } plus data-class default values
implementation_notes: kotlinx.serialization throws SerializationException on unknown keys by default (ignoreUnknownKeys = false), so the pattern is a one-line configuration of the Json format - or the class-level @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys annotation - rather than a structure; the missing-field half comes from data-class default values, which the deserializer uses automatically when a key is absent. Jackson (jackson-module-kotlin) is the alternative when the JSON stack is shared with Java code, but there the tolerance must still be opted into by disabling FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES or annotating with @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true).
code_sketch:
@Serializable
data class Order(val id: String, val total: Long = 0, val lines: Int = 1)

private val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }   // producer may add fields freely

val order = json.decodeFromString<Order>(payload)
pitfalls: The default is strict, so a producer adding a field throws SerializationException at runtime until every consumer's Json instance sets ignoreUnknownKeys = true (or the class carries @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys) - a deploy-order coupling.
Unknown keys are dropped, not preserved: tolerant reading is lossy, so a component that must round-trip the payload needs an explicit JsonObject/explicit-null representation instead.
Defaults cover absent keys but not explicit nulls: a null for a non-nullable property still fails unless coerceInputValues/explicitNulls handling is configured.
